In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how to most economically improve a phylogeny estimate.
the problem of improving the resolution of a phylogeny estimate based on molecular data by adding genes to an existing analysis, but only for a subset of the taxa.

the question of whether a molecular phylogenetist can economically improve the reliability of a phylogenetic hypothesis for a clade of interest by increasing gene sampling, without having the resulting data matrix invalidated by artifacts arising out of the large blocks of missing entries.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, while the phylogeny of Lepidoptera is far from settled, the data set used here has provided the first strong statistical evidence for a number of deep relationships, and that the use of incomplete matrices can be a valuable tool in phylogenetic analysis.
a few dozen genes, sampled in a third of the taxa, is sufficient for a robustly supported phylogeny of the Lepidoptera.
the more data, the better, but that one may safely augment a data set by increasing sampling of some taxa and/or genes without invalidating an initial analysis based on a more complete data set.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, for the Ditrysia, the most promising strategy for resolving deeper relationships is to focus on a few key taxa, using as much gene sampling as possible, while also seeking to increase the total gene sample in a more economical manner.
a modestly augmented gene sample can often be a cost-effective means of improving a molecular phylogenic analysis, even when a substantial fraction of data is missing.

, in a phylogenomic study with a large taxon sampling and a large number of genes, the best strategy may be to sample genes in all taxa, and then to sample taxa in all genes, rather than the other way around.
